limits: THIS GUARD IS A FLOOR AND THIS CONTROL MEASURES THE FLOOR, NOT #775. It establishes that an approved-plan ARTIFACT is present, never that an APPROVAL OCCURRED, and only on the tool paths the hook is matched against. Nothing here should be read as evidence that #775 is enforced - meeting that needs /flow:auto to RECORD Step 3 where a hook can read it before the first edit, which is a command-document change and was deliberately not attempted. THE ANTI-CONTROL PROPERTY IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: bad-no-record-refuses and good-record-present-allows are the SAME fixture differing only in whether the record exists, so a guard that blocked unconditionally would fail the second and a guard that allowed unconditionally would fail the first. A control whose bad case still passes with its planted defect removed is not a weaker control, it is an ANTI-CONTROL - it manufactures confidence - and that is exactly what #1203 found in a real-repo case that still matched with its defect entirely gone. COVERAGE DIFFERS BY AUDIENCE AND BOTH HALVES ARE STATED ON PURPOSE. In THIS fleet coverage is NEAR ZERO, and that is now a MEASUREMENT rather than an estimate: sessions are steered to make file changes through Bash heredocs rather than Write/Edit, so the unseen path is the instructed default. Counted from a single session's own transcript across five delivered issues (#1182, #1191, #1192, #1151 and the S4 re-sync trigger): 468 Bash tool calls against 0 Write, Edit or NotebookEdit calls. The matcher is Write|Edit|NotebookEdit, so this guard would have fired ZERO times over every plan record and every source edit that session made. The earlier figure recorded here - three plan records across three runs, zero via Write - was correct and is superseded rather than corrected: same direction, two orders of magnitude more input. And good-BLIND-bash-redirection-is-NOT-SEEN commits that blindness as a CASE, so a change in the steer or the matcher flips it and the flip is the notification. THE HONEST POSITION, stated because the issue promises 'enforced rather than asserted': enforced for the tool path nobody here uses, asserted for the one everybody does. That is a coverage argument, not a correctness one - the hook does what it says. WHERE IT SHIPS coverage is genuinely useful, because Bash-first steering is a property of how this fleet is operated and not of the hook mechanism. THE RECORD PATH IS THE ONLY EXEMPTION and good-record-path-is-exempt pins it: the record is written BY an edit, so a guard without that exemption blocks the write that would unblock it and every run deadlocks on its first edit. The exemption is a hole - anything able to write the record can write itself an approval - and it is subsumed by the wider Bash hole rather than being the marginal risk. FIXTURES ARE BUILT, NEVER THE LIVE WORKTREE: each case gets a real throwaway git repository outside every checkout with a branch named issue-<N>-<slug>, and the runner REFUSES when TMPDIR sits inside a repository, because a control reading ambient state measures its environment instead of its subject.

anchors.why: There is no pre-fix version of this guard: before #1083 NOTHING enforced #775 - .claude/hooks.json carried one SessionStart notice and two PostToolUse masks, verified in the issue at 5ceb966. So the anchor is the state this replaces, which is the ABSENCE of a guard, vendored as a script that allows everything. Run against these cases it allows the known-bad inputs, which is precisely what the repository did before this change. Provenance reads unverified for that structural reason rather than a temporary one: there is nothing in git history for --verify-provenance to resolve, and there never will be.
